subtopic: Groupthink
passage: Dear Minakshi, You asked how the new job is going. Honestly, I am not sure. In the product meeting last Thursday I said the launch date depended on a part we had not tested. Sanjay said, "Mohit is being negative again," and two others laughed. Deepa, who sits next to me, looked at her notes. Nobody asked what the risk was. Since then I have not spoken in a meeting once, and yesterday I noticed I had stopped raising things at all. I keep asking myself whether I was wrong to say it. I am wondering whether to look for a place where an honest concern is not called negativity. I miss your old team. — Mohit

qa.q: What did Sanjay say after the risk was raised?
qa.a: Sanjay said, "Mohit is being negative again."

qa.q: Why has Mohit stopped raising things in meetings?
qa.a: Mohit has learned that honesty can cost belonging, and feels hurt and doubtful; being called negative made speaking up feel unsafe.

qa.q: What could Mohit try before deciding to leave?
qa.a: Mohit could write the risk down with the facts and send it in writing before the next meeting, or ask for a private talk with someone who listens; that tests whether the team can hear a concern.

qa.q: What might Deepa be feeling while looking at her notes after the laughter?
qa.a: Deepa may feel uncomfortable and unsure; looking away suggests not wanting to join the laughing but also not wanting to be labelled next.

grounding: A team member who raises a risk is called negative, learns that honesty costs belonging, and considers going quiet or leaving.

subtopic: Groupthink
passage: Hemant, you asked why I moved teams. Okay. In my old team every risk I raised got the same answer: "Here comes Ritu." Once I said the vendor's data looked incomplete, and the manager said, "Not a team player, are we?" In front of nine people. Nobody said a word, not even Prakash, who had told me the same thing in private the day before. After that I stopped. I would sit there with a sentence in my mouth and swallow it. My stomach knots even now, telling you. Months later the vendor's data turned out to be incomplete. Nobody called to say sorry. I left the week after.

qa.q: What did the manager say after the vendor's data was called incomplete?
qa.a: The manager said, "Not a team player, are we?"

qa.q: What does Ritu's swallowing of sentences and the knot in the stomach suggest about how Ritu felt in that team?
qa.a: It suggests fear and hurt: Ritu learned that speaking honestly cost belonging, so the feeling became a habit of silence.

qa.q: What could Prakash or another team member have done that day to support Ritu?
qa.a: Prakash could have said out loud what had been said in private, or asked the manager to look at the vendor's data, so Ritu did not stand alone.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Prakash to say nothing after agreeing with Ritu in private?
qa.a: Prakash may have felt guilty and afraid of being labelled too; agreeing privately but not publicly shows how strongly the label kept people quiet.

grounding: A team member who raises a risk is called not a team player, learns that honesty costs belonging, goes quiet and eventually leaves.

subtopic: Groupthink
passage: Sachin, it's Omkar here, and you would not believe the meeting yesterday. Forty minutes, five decisions, and not one person argued. I should have been happy, right? Instead my neck prickled. Kavita, who usually asks a hundred questions, asked none. Rahul just said "fine" to a budget I know worries him. So I stopped the meeting early and said, "From now on I will speak last, and tonight each of you send me one thing that could go wrong." Three emails were in my inbox before I got home. Sachin, quiet had not meant agreed, and I nearly missed it.

qa.q: How many decisions were made in forty minutes?
qa.a: Five decisions were made in forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Omkar's neck prickle instead of feeling happy after the easy meeting?
qa.a: Omkar read the lack of argument as a warning sign; Kavita asking no questions and Rahul's quick "fine" suggested people were not speaking up, so unease replaced relief.

qa.q: What did Omkar change at the end of the meeting to invite honest views?
qa.a: Omkar decided to speak last and asked everyone to send one possible problem that evening, so people could say it in writing.

qa.q: Why might Kavita, who usually asks many questions, have stayed silent?
qa.a: Kavita may have felt the mood made questions unwelcome, or may have assumed others agreed; the silence could hide a concern.

grounding: Someone running a meeting notices that discussions end too easily and reads the silence as a warning that people are not speaking up.

subtopic: Groupthink
passage: I sit two seats from Kiran, so I saw what happened after Tuesday's planning call. Six of us said "fine" to the new schedule in under a minute. Kiran, our manager, did not smile. Kiran looked around the table, tapped a pen twice, and said, "That was too easy. Nikhil, tell me what would break this plan." Nikhil laughed, went red, then said the testing time was too short. Then Meera said the same thing, and then me. I cannot say what Kiran felt at that point; Kiran just wrote things down and said, "Thank you, that is more useful than a yes."

qa.q: How many people said "fine" to the new schedule?
qa.a: Six people said "fine" to the new schedule in under a minute.

qa.q: What might Kiran have been thinking when saying "That was too easy"?
qa.a: Kiran seems to have sensed that quick agreement meant people were holding back, and felt concerned rather than relieved; the narrator cannot be sure of Kiran's exact feeling.

qa.q: What choice by Kiran got real concerns onto the table?
qa.a: Kiran named the easy agreement, asked one person directly what would break the plan, and thanked those who then spoke up.

qa.q: What might Nikhil have been feeling when laughing, going red and then answering?
qa.a: Nikhil probably felt caught off guard and a little embarrassed, but also relieved to have permission to say the testing time was too short.

grounding: A manager senses false harmony when a discussion ends too easily and reads it as people not speaking up, seen by a team member.

subtopic: Groupthink
passage:
Ankita: before we lock the venue plan, Madhuri, can you argue against it tomorrow? Take the other side, whatever you honestly think.
Madhuri: really? I do have a few doubts about the outdoor stage 😅
Ankita: that's exactly what I want. Everyone else, please listen first. I'll speak last.
Dev: ok
Nisha: I like the outdoor stage but fine
(next day)
Madhuri: Rain risk, sound, and only one exit. That's my case.
Nisha: ...the exit thing is actually a real problem
Dev: hadn't thought about the sound
Ankita: Thank you Madhuri. That changed my mind about two things 🙂

qa.q: What three problems did Madhuri name against the outdoor stage?
qa.a: Madhuri named rain risk, sound, and only one exit.

qa.q: Why does Ankita ask Madhuri to argue against the plan and promise to speak last?
qa.a: Ankita wants honest doubts to come out and does not want Ankita's own view to shape the others first, showing a wish to make dissent safe.

qa.q: What did Ankita do after hearing Madhuri that kept the habit alive?
qa.a: Ankita thanked Madhuri and said the argument changed two of Ankita's views, which shows that raising problems is valued, not punished.

qa.q: What might Madhuri feel when asked to take the other side and then thanked?
qa.a: Madhuri probably feels a little nervous at first and then valued, since doubts about the stage were welcome rather than called negative.

grounding: One person planning an event asks someone to argue against the plan, speaks last and thanks the person who raises problems, making dissent safe.

subtopic: Groupthink
passage: In the panchayat hall of a small village, the cooperative's secretary Rajni was about to close the meeting on buying a shared tractor. Fifteen farmers nodded, and the sarpanch spoke loudest in favour. Rajni raised a hand. "Pallavi, you keep the accounts and you always find problems. Please argue against the tractor for five minutes. I will speak last." Pallavi smiled and stood. "Who drives it in the sowing week, who pays for repairs, and what if the rains are late?" The hall shifted. A young farmer, Ganesh, murmured, "She is right." When Rajni finally spoke, it was to say, "Thank you, Pallavi. Now we decide with our eyes open."

qa.q: What did Rajni ask Pallavi to do for five minutes?
qa.a: Rajni asked Pallavi to argue against the tractor for five minutes.

qa.q: Why does Rajni speak last and ask Pallavi to argue against the tractor?
qa.a: Rajni wants the group's confidence tested and does not want to steer the room; the request shows a belief that honest problems protect the cooperative.

qa.q: What did Rajni do at the end that kept dissent normal?
qa.a: Rajni thanked Pallavi and said the decision would now be made with eyes open, treating the problems as help rather than disloyalty.

qa.q: What might Ganesh be feeling when murmuring "She is right"?
qa.a: Ganesh probably feels relieved and a little surprised that the doubts Ganesh may have had were spoken aloud by someone else.

grounding: A cooperative's secretary invites someone to argue against the plan, speaks last and thanks the person who raises problems.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: At the school water fountain Abhinav slipped and fell hard, and his tiffin skidded across the floor. About twenty children were in the corridor. Jaya stood with her water bottle, watching. Everyone else was watching too, and a few whispered. Somebody will go, Jaya thought. Somebody will tell Ma'am. Abhinav sat holding his knee. Nobody moved. A bell rang, and the crowd drifted off in twos and threes. Jaya walked to class with a tight throat, wondering how many of the others had thought exactly the same thing.

qa.q: About how many children were in the corridor when Abhinav fell?
qa.a: About twenty children were in the corridor.

qa.q: What was Jaya thinking while standing with the water bottle?
qa.a: Jaya assumed somebody else would go and tell Ma'am, so the sense of duty felt spread among everyone; afterwards the tight throat shows guilt and unease.

qa.q: What could Jaya do at that moment instead of waiting?
qa.a: Jaya could point at one person, or walk to the nearest teacher and say "Abhinav fell and needs help", since one clear step ends the waiting.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have experienced twenty children watching and nobody coming?
qa.a: Abhinav may have felt embarrassed and alone, holding a hurt knee while everyone watched but no one came near.

grounding: A child sees another child fall and does nothing because many others are watching too, each assuming someone else will step in.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: From the school bus window I saw it. Vandana fell off the swing and sat holding her elbow. About ten children formed a ring around her. Anirban was in it, twisting a shirt button. He looked at the girl next to him, who looked at the boy next to her. Everyone seemed to be waiting for somebody. After a full minute a girl at the back ran off toward the staff room, and the ring melted. I do not know what Anirban was thinking, but he was the last to leave, still looking back at Vandana.

qa.q: What was Anirban doing while standing in the ring?
qa.a: Anirban was twisting a shirt button.

qa.q: What might Anirban have been feeling while looking at the girl next to him?
qa.a: Anirban may have been uneasy and unsure, waiting for someone else to move first; looking back at Vandana suggests some guilt, though the narrator cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Anirban have done in that first minute?
qa.a: Anirban could have pointed to one person and said "You, get Ma'am", or gone to the staff room himself, which breaks the waiting.

qa.q: What might Vandana have experienced during the minute when the ring of children stayed still?
qa.a: Vandana probably felt hurt, embarrassed and alone, sitting with a sore elbow while ten children watched without acting.

grounding: A child sees another child fall and waits for others to act, and a bystander's account shows each assuming someone else will step in.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: In a Melbourne primary school Ms Clarke had taught the class a drill: say "I need help" and point at one adult by name. On Thursday at lunch Zeynep saw two bigger boys take Hiroshi's cap and toss it over the fence while Hiroshi stood with fists tight. A crowd of children watched. Zeynep's heart thumped. "Tattletale" was a word Zeynep had heard before. But Zeynep pointed at the duty teacher and called, "Mr Ellis, I need help, Hiroshi's cap!" He came at once, fetched the cap and stayed with Hiroshi for the rest of lunch. Later Ms Clarke thanked Zeynep and spoke with the two boys.

qa.q: What did Ms Clarke teach the class to say?
qa.a: Ms Clarke taught the class to say "I need help" and point at one adult by name.

qa.q: What was Zeynep feeling before calling Mr Ellis?
qa.a: Zeynep felt nervous, with a thumping heart, and worried about being called a tattletale, but chose to ask for help anyway.

qa.q: What made Zeynep's request work so quickly?
qa.a: Zeynep pointed at a specific adult, Mr Ellis, by name and said exactly what was wrong, so he knew who was needed and why.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi have felt when Mr Ellis came and stayed for the rest of lunch?
qa.a: Hiroshi probably felt relieved and less alone; standing with tight fists before shows how upset and powerless Hiroshi had been.

grounding: A child learns that getting help is caring, not tattling, by practising "I need help" and pointing at one specific adult.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Mrs Kaur had a poster on the wall: "Getting help is caring, not tattling." At break Vikas saw a group of older boys tip Tarun's tiffin into the bin while a ring of children watched and giggled. Tarun stood still, lips tight. Vikas's knees felt weak. He walked to the staffroom door and said, "Mrs Kaur, I need help. Tarun's tiffin is in the bin and the big boys are standing over him." Mrs Kaur put down her tea and followed him at once, sent the boys to the head, and took Tarun to the canteen for a fresh sandwich. That afternoon she also phoned Tarun's family.

qa.q: What did Vikas say at the staffroom door?
qa.a: Vikas said, "Mrs Kaur, I need help. Tarun's tiffin is in the bin and the big boys are standing over him."

qa.q: What might Vikas be feeling as his knees go weak before speaking to Mrs Kaur?
qa.a: Vikas feels frightened and torn about getting involved, but the poster's idea that help is caring pushes him to speak.

qa.q: What turning point made Vikas's help effective?
qa.a: Vikas walked to Mrs Kaur, named her and described exactly what was happening, so she could act at once.

qa.q: What might Tarun have felt when Mrs Kaur arrived and took him to the canteen?
qa.a: Tarun probably felt relieved and cared for, after standing still with tight lips while others giggled.

grounding: A child learns that getting help from a teacher is caring, not tattling, by saying "I need help" to one specific adult.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: I am Gurleen, and I keep going back to the birthday party. My friend Sangeeta sat down on the kitchen floor, pale and swaying, saying the room was spinning. I looked around to see if anyone else thought it was serious. Rohit was laughing at his phone. Two girls were arguing about music. Nobody looked worried, so I told myself Sangeeta was just being dramatic. I stood there with my hands in my pockets. Then Rohit's mother came in for the cake, took one look, sat down beside Sangeeta and phoned Sangeeta's family. I felt my face burn. I had looked at calm faces and decided calm meant fine.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta say was happening in the kitchen?
qa.a: Sangeeta said the room was spinning.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen decide that Sangeeta was just being dramatic?
qa.a: Gurleen looked around for cues and saw calm faces, so assumed it could not be serious; uncertainty was quietly settled by what the crowd showed.

qa.q: What could Gurleen have done when Sangeeta sat down on the floor?
qa.a: Gurleen could have stayed beside Sangeeta and asked directly "are you okay?", then fetched an adult such as Rohit's mother without waiting for anyone else to react.

qa.q: What might Rohit's mother have seen that Gurleen missed?
qa.a: Rohit's mother looked only at Sangeeta, not at the crowd's faces, and saw a pale, swaying child who needed care and an adult's call to Sangeeta's family.

grounding: A teenager sees a friend in trouble at a gathering, checks the calm faces around and decides it must be fine.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Teacher's note. On Wednesday I found Lokesh at the edge of a crowd in the east corridor where two boys were shoving each other. About fifteen students stood around, and nobody had called for a teacher. Lokesh told me later, "I looked at everyone else. They were just standing there, so I thought it must be a normal argument." I walked Lokesh to the office and thanked Lokesh for telling me plainly, and said checking with a teacher is never wrong. The head spoke with both boys the same day. — Rajni

qa.q: About how many students stood around the two boys?
qa.a: About fifteen students stood around the two boys.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh think it must be a normal argument?
qa.a: Lokesh looked around, saw everyone standing calmly, and took that as proof it was not serious; the uncertainty was answered by other people's calm.

qa.q: What turning point in Rajni's response could help Lokesh next time?
qa.a: Rajni thanked Lokesh for being honest and said checking with a teacher is never wrong, which gives Lokesh permission to act on a doubt.

qa.q: How might the two boys who were shoving have experienced fifteen students standing by?
qa.a: They may have felt the crowd was watching and expecting more, or may have felt trapped by the audience; nobody's calm face told them to stop.

grounding: A teenager sees a fight in a group, looks around to check whether it is serious and, seeing calm faces, decides it must be fine.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Rain hammered the bus roof, and Eshaan, late for the maths exam, stood packed between strangers. A woman near the door slid slowly to the floor, eyes closed. Nobody moved. Pallavi, a girl from Eshaan's class, was pressed against the window and mouthed, "Is she asleep?" Eshaan wanted to shout for the driver, but what if she was only tired and everyone laughed at him? The bus lurched. Eshaan checked the watch, then the woman's pale face, and stayed silent. At the next stop an older man knelt beside her and called for help. Eshaan got off at the school gate, ears burning, and could not read the first question. That night sleep would not come.

qa.q: Why was Eshaan on the bus in a hurry?
qa.a: Eshaan was late for the maths exam.

qa.q: Why does Eshaan hold back from shouting for the driver?
qa.a: Eshaan feared looking foolish if the woman was only tired and everyone laughed; the social risk felt bigger than the woman's need in that moment, and guilt came later.

qa.q: What could Eshaan have done at the moment the woman slid to the floor?
qa.a: Eshaan could have asked the woman quietly "are you okay?", or told the driver "someone may be unwell", a small low-risk step that does not need certainty.

qa.q: What might it have been like for the woman on the floor while nobody moved?
qa.a: The woman may have felt frightened or helpless, or may not have been aware at all; the bus stayed silent until an older man knelt beside her.

grounding: A teenager hesitates to help on a crowded bus because of fear of looking foolish, and guilt arrives later.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: At a mall in Delhi, Jasleen and her friend Charu were sharing fries when a toddler in a yellow dress started crying near the escalator, alone. Shoppers streamed past. Jasleen half rose. Then she thought: what if the mother is just around the corner, and I look silly, like I am making a scene? "Someone will come," said Charu, checking her phone. Two minutes passed, then five. The toddler's cries grew hoarse. A guard finally noticed and lifted the child, and a woman ran up, gasping. Jasleen sat back down with her cheeks hot, and the fries tasted like paper.

qa.q: Where was the toddler when crying alone?
qa.a: The toddler was crying alone near the escalator.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen only half rise and then sit down?
qa.a: Jasleen feared looking silly for making a scene if the mother was near; embarrassment outweighed the child's need, and afterwards Jasleen felt guilt.

qa.q: What small step could Jasleen take next time without making a scene?
qa.a: Jasleen could walk over, stay beside the child and quietly tell the nearest guard, a small helpful action even if the parent turns out to be near.

qa.q: What might Charu have been thinking when saying "Someone will come"?
qa.a: Charu probably assumed the child would be noticed by the many people passing and did not want to overreact; the phone gave a way to avoid deciding.

grounding: A teenager hesitates to help because of fear of looking foolish if the situation is misread, and guilt arrives later.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Sarika, it's Sachin, and I have to say this out loud once. In the corridor before assembly, Nikhil and his group kept grabbing my bag and throwing it around, calling me names. There were maybe thirty people there. Some stared at their phones, some looked at the floor, and two laughed. Not one said stop. That silence felt worse than the names. I felt like a piece of furniture. You were the only one who found me at the water tap, and you did not ask anything, you just sat there. Then you said, "Come with me to the counsellor." She listened, said it was not my fault, and called my class teacher and my family that same afternoon.

qa.q: About how many people were in the corridor?
qa.a: There were maybe thirty people in the corridor.

qa.q: Why did the silence feel worse than the names to Sachin?
qa.a: The silence made Sachin feel alone and invisible, like a piece of furniture, as if nobody saw the harm as real.

qa.q: What turning point helped Sachin that day?
qa.a: Sarika sat quietly at the water tap and then took Sachin to the counsellor, who listened, said it was not Sachin's fault, and called the class teacher and family that afternoon.

qa.q: What might Sarika have been feeling when finding Sachin at the water tap and sitting without asking anything?
qa.a: Sarika probably felt concerned and unsure what to say, and chose company over questions so that Sachin would not feel pushed.

grounding: A student being harassed notices that many people see it and nobody speaks; the silence hurts, and an adult responds the same day.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: My name is Chandrika, and I saw it on the school bus home. Two boys in the back seat kept flicking paper balls at Sangeeta and calling out about her hair. The bus was full, maybe twenty-five of us. Nobody said a word. A few people put in earphones and turned to the window. Sangeeta pressed her forehead to the glass and hugged her bag, and her shoulders shrank a little more at every stop. I felt frozen in my seat too. At the market stop I made myself stand up, sat down beside her and called Mrs Rao, the bus attendant, to the back. Mrs Rao moved the boys to the front, stayed near Sangeeta for the rest of the ride and phoned the principal, who said the boys' families would be called that evening. Sangeeta did not say much, but she let me keep the seat.

qa.q: Where did the boys pick on Sangeeta?
qa.a: On the school bus home, where two boys in the back seat flicked paper balls at Sangeeta and called out about her hair.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta have been feeling with her forehead pressed to the glass?
qa.a: Sangeeta was probably humiliated and alone; hugging her bag and shrinking at every stop suggests the silence of the full bus hurt as much as the boys' words.

qa.q: What turning point came at the market stop?
qa.a: Chandrika stood up, sat beside Sangeeta and called Mrs Rao, who moved the boys, stayed near Sangeeta and phoned the principal.

qa.q: What was it like for Chandrika to sit frozen while the paper balls kept flying?
qa.a: Chandrika seems to have felt stuck and uneasy, part of the silent crowd, until standing up broke that silence.

grounding: A student being picked on sees a whole bus watch in silence, and a fellow passenger's account shows how that silence isolates her until someone steps in and adults respond the same day.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Pooja, you asked how I did it. Honestly, I was terrified. It's Ayesha, remember. At the bus-stop shelter an older guy kept crowding a girl who was gripping her bag, and everyone was looking at their phones. I did not shout. I walked up and said, "Hey, there you are!" as if I knew her, and asked her to sit with me. She did, fast. The guy hovered a bit, then wandered off when I stared at the timetable really hard. When the bus came I told the conductor to keep an eye out for her stop. Small stuff. But I keep thinking, I did not have to fight anyone.

qa.q: What did Ayesha say to the girl at the bus stop?
qa.a: Ayesha said, "Hey, there you are!" as if they already knew each other, and asked her to sit down.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when walking up to the girl?
qa.a: Ayesha was terrified but chose a low-risk action; the words "honestly, I was terrified" show the fear was real even though the action was small.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha's approach work without a confrontation?
qa.a: Ayesha gave the girl a way out and a companion, and asked the conductor to look out for her stop, small safe steps rather than an all-or-nothing act of heroism.

qa.q: What might the girl have felt when Ayesha said "Hey, there you are!" and offered a seat?
qa.a: The girl probably felt relief and safety; sitting fast suggests she was glad someone had noticed and given her an easy way to leave the situation.

grounding: A teenager chooses a low-risk action such as checking on the target and distracting the aggressor, showing safe helping is a range of options.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: I was on the metro platform watching everything, and here is what I saw. A man had grabbed a boy's phone out of a group of schoolkids and was jeering at them. Six or seven commuters stood around. Jahnavi, a girl in a college lanyard, did not shout. She walked up to the boy, asked, "Are you okay? Do you want to call someone?" and stood next to him. Deepika, another passenger, quietly pressed the help button at the pillar and spoke to the station staff. The man saw the two of them and the staff coming and dropped the phone. Jahnavi stayed beside the boy until the guard arrived.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi ask the boy?
qa.a: Jahnavi asked, "Are you okay? Do you want to call someone?"

qa.q: Why might Jahnavi have chosen to stand next to the boy instead of shouting?
qa.a: Jahnavi seems to want to help calmly and safely, showing care for the boy first; standing beside him signals support without provoking the man.

qa.q: What small action by Deepika made a difference?
qa.a: Deepika pressed the help button and told the station staff, a low-risk action that brought adults in without any confrontation.

qa.q: What might the boy have been feeling before and after Jahnavi stood beside him?
qa.a: The boy was probably scared and embarrassed before, and relieved afterwards that someone checked on him and stayed until the guard arrived.

grounding: A teenager and another passenger choose low-risk actions, checking on the target and calling for help, seen by a bystander.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Mentor's note, hostel year group. On Monday Nandini came to me shaken. A cruel post about a first-year had sat in the 120-member hostel chat for six hours, with forty reactions and no reports. Nandini said, "I saw it in the morning and thought somebody must have flagged it already." The sender, Ojas, had not been named by anyone. Nandini realised each reader had thought the same. We reported it to the warden together that hour, and the warden spoke with the first-year and the sender before evening. I told Nandini that assuming someone else has reported is very common, and that being the one who does is useful, not silly. — Meena Ma'am

qa.q: How many members were in the hostel chat?
qa.a: The hostel chat had 120 members.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when coming to the mentor on Monday?
qa.a: Nandini was shaken and guilty, having assumed someone else would report the post; realising everyone had thought the same made the assumption feel heavy.

qa.q: What turning point did Nandini and the mentor take that hour?
qa.a: They reported the post to the warden together straight away, and the warden spoke with the first-year and the sender before evening.

qa.q: What might the first-year have been going through during the six hours the post stayed in the chat?
qa.a: The first-year may have felt exposed and humiliated with no sign anyone cared, as forty people reacted and nobody reported.

grounding: A student sees a cruel post in a big group chat and assumes someone else will report it, since the bigger the group the smaller each person's felt duty.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Saturday. Somebody put a photo of Vandana with a cruel caption in the big class chat, ninety people. My thumb hovered over the report button. Then I thought: with ninety of us, surely someone has already done it. I put the phone down and made tea. An hour later the photo was still there and Vandana had left the chat. That was when I felt sick. I hit report, then messaged Vandana: "I saw it. I am sorry I waited. Do you want to tell our class teacher together?" She wrote back "ok". We called the teacher that evening. The teacher answered, asked for screenshots, and got the post taken down before night. — Anirban

qa.q: How many people were in the class chat?
qa.a: The class chat had ninety people.

qa.q: Why did Anirban put the phone down without reporting the photo?
qa.a: Anirban assumed that with ninety people someone else must have reported it, so the felt duty was small; the sick feeling came later when Vandana left the chat.

qa.q: What choice did Anirban make once the sick feeling arrived?
qa.a: Anirban reported the photo, apologised to Vandana and offered to call the class teacher together, which turned regret into action.

qa.q: What might Vandana have felt when leaving the chat and later reading Anirban's message?
qa.a: Vandana was probably hurt and humiliated on leaving, and may have felt some comfort at the message, though the plain "ok" shows caution.

grounding: A student sees a cruel post in a big group chat and assumes someone else will report it, then acts once the harm is clear.
